ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First look at the image: This is a square with side length 1. There is a larger circle in the lower left, tangent to the left side and bottom side of the square; there is a smaller circle in the upper right, tangent to the top side and right side of the square; the two circles are tangent to each other, and their centers both lie on the same diagonal of the square from lower left to upper right. Use the coordinate method to handle it. Let the square be [0,1]×[0,1]. If the radius of the large circle is R, because it is tangent to the left side and bottom side, its center is (R,R). If the radius of the small circle is r, because it is tangent to the top side and right side, its center is (1-r,1-r). The two circles are externally tangent, so the distance between the two centers equals R+r. From the coordinates, the distance between the two centers is sqrt((1-r-R)^2+(1-r-R)^2)=sqrt(2)·(1-(R+r)). Let S=R+r, then sqrt(2)(1-S)=S. Solving gives S = sqrt(2)/(1+sqrt(2)) = 2-sqrt(2).

method.method_draft: Use a coordinate setup. Read from the image that the larger circle touches the left and bottom sides of the square, while the smaller circle touches the top and right sides, and their centers lie on the same bottom-left to top-right diagonal. From the text, take the square side length as 1. Put the square as [0,1]×[0,1]. If the large radius is R, its center is (R,R). If the small radius is r, its center is (1-r,1-r). Since the circles touch each other externally, the distance between centers equals R+r. Thus sqrt((1-r-R)^2+(1-r-R)^2)=R+r, so sqrt(2)(1-(R+r))=R+r. Let S=R+r and solve S=sqrt(2)(1-S), giving S=2-sqrt(2).

method.method_draft: Use a diagonal-length decomposition. From the image, identify the relevant diagonal as the one from the lower-left corner to the upper-right corner, with the large circle near the lower-left corner and the small circle near the upper-right corner. From the text, the square side length is 1, so this diagonal has length sqrt(2). Let the radii be R and r. Along the diagonal, the distance from the lower-left corner to the large circle’s center is R sqrt(2), because the center is R from both adjacent sides. Similarly, the distance from the small circle’s center to the upper-right corner is r sqrt(2). Since the two circles touch, the distance between their centers is R+r. These three collinear pieces fill the square diagonal: R sqrt(2)+(R+r)+r sqrt(2)=sqrt(2). Therefore (sqrt(2)+1)(R+r)=sqrt(2), so R+r=2-sqrt(2).

sqrt((1-r-R)^2+(1-r-R)^2)

claims.claim: sqrt((1-r-R)^2+(1-r-R)^2) simplifies to sqrt(2)·(1-(R+r)).
claims.label: reasoning

claims.claim: Let S=R+r.
claims.label: reasoning
claims.source: Let S=R+r

claims.claim: S satisfies the equation sqrt(2)(1-S)=S.
claims.label: reasoning
claims.source:
Then there is
sqrt(2)(1-S)=S

claims.claim: Solving gives S = sqrt(2)/(1+sqrt(2)).
claims.label: reasoning
claims.source: Solving gives S = sqrt(2)/(1+sqrt(2))

claims.claim: sqrt(2)/(1+sqrt(2)) = 2-sqrt(2)。
claims.label: reasoning
claims.source: sqrt(2)/(1+sqrt(2)) = 2-sqrt(2)

claims.claim: The sum of the radii of the two circles is 2-sqrt(2).
claims.label: reasoning
